metadata.note: The Canandaigua and Niagara Falls Railroad, later the New York Central's 'Peanut Line'. Chartered in 1851 and opened through on July 1 1853, it ran west from Canandaigua on the Auburn Road through Honeoye Falls, Caledonia, Le Roy, Batavia, Akron and Clarence Center to North Tonawanda, and on to Niagara Falls and the Suspension Bridge. Its distinguishing feature was its gauge: it was laid to 6 feet to match the Erie Railroad, and its purpose was to give the Erie a broad-gauge connection to Niagara Falls and the new bridge over the gorge. That lasted five years. The company was bought out by its creditors in 1857, reorganised as the Niagara Bridge and Canandaigua Railroad on Aug 25 1858, and leased to the New York Central on Sept 1 1858, which regauged it to standard and so shut the Erie out of Niagara Falls by this route. Merged into the NYC in 1890, it was worked as the Tonawanda and Batavia branches but was always the 'Peanut', after NYC vice-president Dean Richmond called it 'only a peanut of a line'. Passenger service ended in 1933, the eastern half was abandoned in January 1939, and the last fragment went in January 1978. Setting the map's year slider across 1858 shows the line change from Erie broad-gauge black to New York Central grey.
sources: https://nyrails.org/?page_id=2745 (New York Central 'Peanut Line'). Station sequence used for the route: North Tonawanda, Getzville, Transit, Clarence Center, East Clarence, Parkers, Akron Junction, Akron Falls, Falkirk, Pembroke, Indian Road Crossing, Pembroke Center, East Pembroke, Batavia, Stafford, Le Roy, Lime Rock, Caledonia, Maxwells, Golah, West Rush, Honeoye Falls, West Bloomfield, Ionia, Holcomb, Wheeler's Siding, Canandaigua. Also: the Canandaigua and Niagara Falls Railroad was completed July 1 1853 and laid to six-foot gauge to interface with the Erie; purchased by creditors' representatives 1857, reorganised as the Niagara Bridge and Canandaigua Railroad 1858 and leased to the New York Central, which converted it to standard gauge and merged it in 1890; operated as the Tonawanda and Batavia branches; nicknamed by NYC vice-president Dean Richmond as 'only a peanut of a line'; passenger service ceased 1933. Abandonment dates by segment: Holcomb-Caledonia (23.15 mi) Jan 14 1939; North Tonawanda-Transit (9.35 mi) 1956; Brixment-Akron Junction (1.78 mi) 1961; Batavia-Pembroke (12.82 mi) 1962; Transit-Getzville (3.56 mi) 1963; Canandaigua-Holcomb (8.07 mi) 1972; Batavia-P&L Junction Feb 1975; Akron Junction-Transit (8.6 mi) Jan 7 1978.

https://www.crookedlakereview.com/articles/136_150/142springsummer2007/142sheret.html ('The Peanut Line of the New York Central Railroad' by John G. Sheret): organising meeting at Lima, N.Y. Mar 4 1851; first train reached Honeoye Falls Jan 1 1853; extended to Niagara Falls July 1 1853; first excursion train over the whole route July 28 1853; originally six-foot gauge, changed to standard shortly after New York Central acquisition; passenger service ended 1933 with two or three passengers per trip; final freight run Jan 15 1939, when old-time residents lined the track.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_and_Niagara_Falls_Railroad and related NYC coverage (the first stage opened in 1853 from Canandaigua on the Auburn Road west to Batavia on the main line, continuing to North Tonawanda later that year and reaching the Niagara Falls Suspension Bridge in 1854; the six-foot gauge let it connect with the Erie, giving the Erie access to Niagara Falls; reorganised Aug 25 1858 as the Niagara Bridge and Canandaigua Railroad, leased to the New York Central Sept 1 1858 and regauged, depriving the Erie of its broad-gauge connection).
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Timetable frequencies and speeds for every era are estimates. Sources differ on when the New York Central took control -- the Crooked Lake Review article says 1855 or 1857 depending on the account, while nyrails gives the 1857 creditor purchase and the 1858 reorganisation and lease followed here. No per-station mileposts were found, so the geometry is checked against crow-flight distance leg by leg and against the roughly 90-mile Canandaigua-North Tonawanda length, not against booked mileage. The 1939-1978 feature draws the whole route even though only disconnected stubs survived those years; the individual stub abandonment dates are recorded in that feature's segment note but are not drawn separately.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap via Overpass API, shortest-path search over the OSM rail graph between the stations listed above. Routed in three passes -- preferring live rail, preferring abandoned corridors, and preferring abandoned corridors with a wide gap stitch -- keeping the best result per leg. Nearly all of this corridor was abandoned between 1939 and 1978, so most legs depend on OSM's abandoned-railway geometry rather than active track.

Result: 11 of 16 legs followed real track, giving 175 km. metadata.freight_only_audit: REMOVED 2026-08-24 (second pass). Two segments of nyc-peanut-line asserted passenger service that did not exist: 1933-1939, whose own note began 'Freight only.', and 1939-1978, whose note said 'Only disconnected stubs survived' and admitted 'this feature draws the whole route for these years, which overstates what was actually still in place'. Passenger service on the Peanut ended in 1933 and the feature now ends there. WHY THE FIRST AUDIT MISSED IT: the documented re-check grep in data/CONVENTIONS.md is case-sensitive and matches 'freight[- ]only', but this note is capitalised -- 'Freight only.' A case-insensitive re-scan of the whole repo found this one feature and no others; every other freight mention is legitimate end-of-era context. Consequence of the bug: the map drew a through Canandaigua - Batavia - Niagara Falls passenger line for 1977, 45 years after its last passenger train, over trackage much of which had already been lifted.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.nyc_company_split: 2026-08-24: compound "predecessor / New York Central Railroad" company strings split per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. The legend groups on the exact company string (app.js railroadsInView), so a compound string drew as a separate railroad from the New York Central even for years the NYC itself ran the trains. Each feature is now split at the date its own segment note names the new operator, into features with identical geometry: the predecessor keeps its name and colour for the earlier years, and the NYC-operated years become "New York Central Railroad" at #5C677D. The Pittsburgh and Lake Erie and the Big Four were renamed but NOT split -- both were NYC-controlled yet stayed separately operated railroads under their own names, so they keep their own legend row. The 1858-1890 lease era and the post-1890 Peanut Line era became the same company under this change and briefly carried the same label; the later feature now uses the line's own advertised name (Rule 6) rather than its terminals, so the two eras stay distinguishable on hover. They are kept as separate features rather than merged because each carries its own avg_speed_kmh.
